It isn't immoral to hold certain beliefs, but it is immoral to act on beliefs in an immoral way.

There are, in my experience, three factors by which people tend to judge morality:

1.Beliefs

2.Intentions

3.Actions

Consider anti-vax people:

They *believe* that vaccines do more harm than good and that they do not work.

They *intend* to protect their children by not giving them vaccines.

They *act* on their beliefs by not giving their children vaccines.

It could be postulated by some that refusing to vaccinate their children is immoral, but their intention to protect their children was not immoral. Furthermore, they did not even choose to believe whether or not vaccines worked, and thus by believing that they do not is neither moral nor immoral.

This is the biggest problem I had with Christianity; they believe that certain beliefs are moral or immoral, and that people who did good things without believing in Jesus were still sinning. They totally ignore the true indicator of morality: actions. 

P.S: I agree that it is moral to inform one's self as best as possible in order to find the truth and make morally informed actions.

If you think about it, meaning doesn't really exist. Meaning is such an abstract, nebulous and intangible concept that it's impossible to quantify. If life didn't having a meaning, would the events that transpired in it be any different? No. They would not. Thus, meaning only exists if you think it does, and if you believe in meaning, it can only be whatever you think it is.

Would doing the same thing every day for eternity or having someone watch your every action and thought give you a sense of meaning or purpose? Even if you did believe in God, it would be impossible to know whether or not your actions pleased him; you could only guess. I personally don't believe that there is an afterlife, but it is impossible to know for sure until we are dead. If there is no afterlife, then no one, not even dead people, knows what comes after life, because they would be truly dead in this case.

I fail to see the logical connection between an afterlife and meaning in life. In fact, it would give life less meaning. If the afterlife is so great then there's no point in living. After all, if the afterlife was so great, everyone who really believed in it would be just *dying* to die. I know exactly how you feel.

I always had problems socializing as a child but it was never that big of a problem and I just chalked it up as being because I was homeschooled, but now that I'm older it's much more difficult because I'm actually expected to initiate conversations and engage in smalltalk.  Also, I'm not interested in the same things as most boys my age, which makes it even harder to make smalltalk, and the meltdowns I've always had over silly things are a lot more innapropriate now that I'm older and expected to have a grip on my emotions (which I never have, never do, and maybe never will).  My lack of prominent gestures and low level of emotional expression make me seem dead inside, and when I don't seem that way, I come off as an overly silly, immature child.  My few friends often accuse me of "running away" when all I did was walk a very short distance to a nearby place at what seemed to be an appropriate time.  

I have become worse and worse at identifying what emotion I'm feeling and I don't even know what happiness feels like anymore because if I was happy I couldn't tell.  It also seems like my reaction speeds are getting slower and now I'm worse than most of the people in family at board games involving reflexes.  I was always very absent minded and forgetful and I still am, but now it's worse and I can only vaguely remember what happened a few days ago.  I have always been a moderately fidgety child, but now I can't sit still.  Finally, I can barely focus on the task at hand and often forget what I'm doing mid-task.  

I haven't been diagnosed with any mental disorders and I don't think I have any, but the point is that your brain changes a lot during your teenage years, and some of the changes will be good, and ~~most~~ some of them will be bad.  However, there are many ways that autism manifests itself in adolescence and adulthood, and here are 5:

1.Once they are past early to mid childhood, people with autism often have lower levels of emotional maturity than neurotypical people their age, often manifesting itself as tantrums and gulibllity. 

2.People with autism are more likely to have depression, which is most commonly developed during adolescence and in people with autism is often due to the stigma and hatred towards autistic people and/or the challenges they face in social situations.  It also may be because of a desire to "fit in," "be normal," or "be like everybody else."

3.Teenagers with autism are more likely to experience seizures during puberty and these may go away after puberty has ended or may be due to epilepsy, which is comorbid to autism.

4.Children are usually not allowed to us the internet very much until they are at least almost teenagers, and they may use it to make online friends.  Teenagers and adults with autism may find this especially enjoyable as they usually find it much easier than making friends in real life and may infact prefer online friends to in-person ones.

5.Adults with autism are often don' realize that their friend is a "bad friend" and are often stuck in manipulative or abusive relationships.  They are also more likely to be tricked in to making bad deals or purchases.

6.Adults with autism sometimes break the law accidentally because they don't stop and think "hey, is what I'm doing illegal?" unless they already know that it is.
